To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) The prevalence of C. difficile colonization in the general population is 3%, and 2) The prevalence of symptomatic C. difficile infection is 0.5% of the general population.

(a) C. difficile infection can cause severe disease in patients with a history of inflammatory bowel disease; (b) C. difficile is a frequent cause of relapse of inflammatory bowel disease in patients with quiescent disease; and (c) C. difficile may cause a severe colitis in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
the combination of vancomycin and rifaximin, in the form of an oral suspension, is a safe and effective treatment for antibiotic associated diarrhea caused by Clostrium difficile.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular biology of C. difficile, a pathogen responsible for antibiotic associated diarrhea and pseudomembran colitis.
the development of a novel approach to the diagnosis and treatment of C. difficile infection.
the use of probiotic bacteria to prevent and treat antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the antibiotic treatment of CDAD should not be based on the results of in vitro susceptibility testing, but should rather be based on a clinical judgment, taking the severity of disease, the patient’s condition, and the risk of complications into account.
C. difficile causes antibiotic-associated colitis and is a significant nosocomial pathogen.

the use of probiotics is a safe and effective treatment of antibiotic associated diarrhea (AAD), and the most important probiotic strains for this purpose are Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Saccharomyces boulardii, although the use of other probiotics may be beneficial as well.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that a combination of the antibiotics metronidazole and rifaximin can eradicate the C. difficile infection in 90% of cases, with a low rate of relapse and without the adverse events that have been associated with the use of other antibiotic therapies for C. difficile infection.

the use of probiotic supplements can help prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea and C. difficile infection, and that probiotic supplementation may be a useful adjunctive treatment for C. difficile infection.
C. difficile is a Gram positive spore-forming anaerobic bacillus, and is a normal commensal in the human gastrointestinal tract.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of probiotic bacteria in the management of Clostridiumdifficile infections should be based on a solid understanding of the ecology of the gut and the mechanisms by which the probiotic bacteria exert their beneficial effects, as well as on the specific characteristics of the probiotic strains used.

the current standard of care for C. difficile infection is inadequate, and that we need to develop better treatments, said lead author David Rasko, PhD, assistant professor of microbiology and immunology at the Medical College of Wisconsin.
the use of probiotics is a promising strategy to prevent C. difficile infection, especially in high-risk populations such as the elderly.
